analysis.one_liner: Restricts out-of-state and bundled campaign money, caps House spending, bans soft money, and cuts candidates' TV ad rates.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; referred to four House committees in December 1995, it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for financing House campaigns. It capped the share of a House candidate's money that can come from out-of-state donors at half, banned check-wrapping middlemen who bundle contributions, and banned unregulated 'soft money' payments by parties, corporations, and unions for mixed political activities. It gave taxpayers a credit of up to $100 ($200 for couples) for campaign contributions, set a $500,000 voluntary spending cap and a $25,000 cap on candidates' personal money, and required broadcasters to sell candidates airtime at steep discounts, with license revocation for stations that deny access. It also imposed new taxes and restrictions on the political spending of labor, agricultural, and horticultural organizations.
analysis.who_benefits: House candidates who depend on small in-state donors would have gained from the out-of-state cap, the anti-bundling rule, and the soft money ban, and ordinary taxpayers could have used a $100-per-person tax credit to fund campaigns. Voters would have gained from cheaper, guaranteed candidate airtime and less unregulated party and corporate money in elections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small donors and underfunded House candidates

how_it_helps.text: A House candidate could accept no more than 50% of contributions in a reporting period from people other than individual residents of the candidate's own state, limiting the influence of out-of-state and national money in local elections.
No person could act as an intermediary or conduit for a contribution made by check or negotiable instrument payable to a federal candidate, closing a common bundling loophole.

Payments by party committees, corporations, and labor organizations for 'mixed political activities' such as voter registration drives or general political advertising would have been subject to contribution limits and reporting, and could be paid only from accounts governed by federal campaign law — a ban on soft money.
Individuals could claim a tax credit of up to $100 ($200 on joint returns) for federal campaign contributions, lowering the cost for ordinary people to participate.

Candidates who accepted a $500,000 spending cap and a $25,000 cap on personal funds would get discounts: broadcasters could charge them no more than half the lowest rate for the same airtime, could not preempt their purchased ads, and could lose their license for denying candidates reasonable access on the terms given their most favored advertiser.
If a self-funded opponent spent more than $50,000 of personal money, the in-state contribution limit would be lifted for the eligible candidate's in-state donors.

analysis.who_pays: Labor, agricultural, and horticultural organizations would face new taxes on lobbying and political expenditures and could lose tax exemption for campaign activity. Broadcasters would give up premium ad rates during campaign periods. Wealthy self-funded candidates and large out-of-state donors would lose spending freedom, and national and state party committees would lose the soft money channel.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unions, broadcasters, big donors, and parties

drawbacks.text: The tax provisions single out labor, agricultural, and horticultural organizations (section 501(c)(5) groups) for new taxes on lobbying and political expenditures and for potential loss of tax exemption over campaign activity, while leaving corporate political spending outside the soft money ban largely untouched — a restriction critics would call one-sided against organized labor.

The $500,000 spending cap, even indexed to inflation, could seriously disadvantage candidates in expensive media markets, and the out-of-state contribution cap could hurt candidates in districts near state lines or in media markets spanning states.

The broadcast provisions force stations to sell candidate airtime at half the lowest rate for eligible candidates and threaten license revocation for access violations, a cost stations would bear during every election cycle.
The tax credit for contributions is a federal revenue cost, and its benefit flows to people who already have cash to give, providing little to those who cannot afford to donate at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design — capping outside money, banning soft money, and making candidates pay half-price for airtime in exchange for voluntary spending limits — targets the main channels through which concentrated money reaches House elections, and the tax credit plus reduced postage would make participation cheaper for small donors. The serious flaw is asymmetric: the political-expenditure tax regime applies to unions and agricultural organizations but has no parallel restriction on corporate political activity beyond the soft money rule, so the bill would disarm one set of political actors more than another. The spending and broadcast provisions also raise practical and constitutional questions — the Supreme Court held in Buckley v. Valeo (1976) that mandatory candidate spending limits violate the First Amendment, which is why schemes like this one are framed as 'voluntary' with benefits attached, a design that has drawn sustained legal challenge.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in four House committees and then two subcommittees without ever getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Phil English of Pennsylvania introduced the bill on December 22, 1995, with Rep. Steve Horn as its sole cosponsor.

The same day, the Speaker referred it to four committees — House Oversight, Ways and Means, Commerce, and Government Reform and Oversight — a split referral that meant several committees would each have to act on the provisions in their jurisdiction.
In early January 1996 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Postal Service and the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance; neither took action.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because none of the reforms took effect, the existing campaign money system was preserved: out-of-state donors, contribution bundlers, and party committees spending soft money continued under the old rules, and broadcasters kept charging candidates their regular rates during election periods.

for.name: Rep. Phil English
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Campaign Finance Reform, Fairness, and Citizens Involvement Act on December 22, 1995.

for.name: Rep. Steve Horn
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: House committee and subcommittee leadership
against.role: Chairmen of House Oversight, Ways and Means, Commerce, Government Reform and Oversight, and their subcommittees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral but never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee without any action in the 18 months before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opposition is recorded; the bill had only a Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, so its support never grew past the introduction stage.

industries.note: The bill strips their tax-exempt protection from campaign intervention, taxes their excess lobbying and political expenditures, and allows injunctions and termination assessments for 'flagrant' political spending. Unions are a collective voice for working people in politics, but their unregulated spending is also part of the money-in-politics problem the bill targets.

Stations would have to sell candidate airtime at the lowest rate — and at half that rate for eligible House candidates — during the 30 days before primaries and 60 days before general elections, with no preemption of paid candidate ads and license revocation for denying access. Their premium election-season ad rates are financed by candidates and, ultimately, by donors.

industries.industry: Large out-of-state donors and contribution bundlers
industries.note: The bill caps out-of-state money at half of a House candidate's contributions and bans check-bundling conduits, directly cutting the leverage of national money over local House races.

industries.industry: National and state political parties (soft money)
industries.note: Party spending on mixed activities like voter registration and general political advertising would become a limited, reported expenditure under federal campaign law, closing the soft money loophole; the bill also repeals the party building-fund exception.

Candidates agreeing to the program face a $25,000 cap on personal funds and a $500,000 overall spending cap, though the contribution limit lifts for opponents who spend more than $50,000 of their own money.
